planting.note: Fall-sow onto bare, undisturbed mineral soil since seed needs light and surface contact to germinate, or set out container plugs in early spring; the species dominates vast stretches of the Great Basin and defines the sagebrush steppe ecosystem.

directions: Big sagebrush is the signature evergreen shrub of the Great Basin high desert, forming the structural backbone of sagebrush steppe plant communities from Nevada and Utah north through Idaho and eastern Oregon. Silvery, three-lobed aromatic leaves persist year-round and release a pungent, resinous scent when brushed, while tiny yellow flower heads appear on upright spikes in late summer and fall. It demands sharply drained, unamended soil and essentially no supplemental irrigation once established, and it resents heavy clay, regular watering, or fertile garden beds, which shorten its life and invite root rot. Give it room to spread and avoid crowding it with moisture-loving companions in a mixed native planting.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall so hard seed coats undergo natural cold, moist stratification over winter, burying seed shallowly to deter rodent caching losses; germination is slow and uneven even under good conditions.

directions: Antelope bitterbrush is a deciduous, three-lobed-leaved shrub scattered through sagebrush steppe and adjoining pine woodlands of the Great Basin, prized by wildlife managers as critical winter browse for mule deer and antelope. Small, fragrant pale-yellow flowers resembling tiny roses open in late spring along the twiggy, gray-barked branches, followed by narrow achene fruits. It thrives in lean, rocky, or sandy soils with excellent drainage and needs no irrigation beyond establishment watering, but it is intolerant of heavy or poorly drained ground. Established plants can be lightly thinned in late winter to remove dead wood, though heavy pruning is rarely needed.

planting.note: Direct sow fresh seed shallowly in fall, since viability drops quickly in storage and seed germinates readily in cool temperatures without pretreatment; thin seedlings to their final spacing the following spring.

directions: Winterfat is a low, silvery-haired subshrub of alkaline flats and sagebrush steppe across the Great Basin, named for the dense white-woolly seed clusters that persist through winter and provide valuable forage when other browse is buried in snow. Narrow gray-green leaves and felted stems give the whole plant a soft, frosted appearance that stands out against the darker sagebrush around it. It is exceptionally drought- and cold-tolerant, thriving in saline or alkaline soils that few other ornamentals accept, and needs no supplemental water once rooted. Cut plants back by a third every few years to prevent the woody base from becoming sparse and leggy.

planting.note: Fall-sow to let winter moisture break the hard seed coat, or nick and soak seed before spring sowing; direct-seed into lean, well-drained soil since the deep taproot resents transplanting once established.

directions: Munro's globemallow is a gray-felted, mallow-flowered perennial common on dry rangeland, roadsides, and disturbed sagebrush steppe throughout the Great Basin and interior Pacific Northwest. Clusters of apricot-orange, saucer-shaped flowers line the upright stems from late spring into midsummer and draw a steady traffic of native bees, including globemallow bee specialists. It is extremely drought-tolerant and actually declines with regular watering or rich soil, performing best in lean, gravelly or sandy ground in full sun. Shear plants back hard after bloom to encourage a tidier rebloom and to keep the often short-lived perennial vigorous for another season.

planting.note: Dormant-seed in fall just before freeze-up so seed overwinters in cool, moist soil ahead of spring growth, a standard practice for establishing this cool-season bunchgrass in Great Basin restoration plantings.

directions: Bluebunch wheatgrass is the dominant native bunchgrass of Great Basin sagebrush steppe, forming dense, arching tufts of fine blue-green foliage beneath and between sagebrush and bitterbrush shrubs. Slender seed heads with distinctively spaced, overlapping spikelets rise well above the foliage in early summer and cure to a warm tan by fall. As a cool-season grass it grows most actively in spring and fall, going summer-dormant in the driest months, and it tolerates heavy grazing and drought far better than most introduced pasture grasses. Use it in native meadow plantings, erosion-control seedings, or as a textural companion to sagebrush-steppe wildflowers, and avoid summer irrigation that encourages weedy competition.
sources: Bureau of Land Management Seeds of Success

planting.note: Dormant-seed in late fall so freeze-thaw cycles over winter break seed dormancy naturally, drilling shallowly into sandy or gravelly soil; spring-sown seed germinates far less reliably without this chilling period.

directions: Indian ricegrass (long known under the synonym Oryzopsis hymenoides) is a fine-textured, airy bunchgrass of sandy and gravelly sites throughout the Great Basin sagebrush steppe, often found growing right through the canopy of big sagebrush and bitterbrush. Delicate, open panicles of large, rounded seeds nod above the narrow, rolled blue-green leaves from late spring into summer, and the plump seeds were historically an important food source ground into flour. It is among the most drought-tolerant native grasses, thriving in pure sand and requiring no irrigation once established, but it struggles in heavy clay or poorly drained soils. Leave seed heads standing through fall for wildlife and self-sowing, and avoid mowing until seed has shattered.

planting.note: Fall-sow onto sharply drained, gritty soil and let winter cold stratify the seed naturally, since germination is slow and uneven even under good conditions; container divisions can also be set out in spring.

directions: Cushion buckwheat forms tight, silvery mats of small spoon-shaped leaves on dry ridges, gravel bars, and open ground within the Great Basin sagebrush steppe, often on sites too harsh for sagebrush itself. Rounded flower heads in shades of cream, pink, or yellow rise on short leafless stalks just above the foliage mat in late spring and early summer, feeding a wide range of native bees and butterflies. It demands gritty, extremely well-drained soil and dislikes any summer moisture around its crown, making it a natural fit for rock gardens, gravel beds, and crevice plantings rather than irrigated borders. Leave old flower stalks in place through winter for seed dispersal and visual interest.

planting.note: Direct sow in spring into lean, well-drained soil, since seed germinates readily without pretreatment; this shrubby mustard often appears on disturbed, mineral-rich ground and tolerates soils too alkaline or seleniferous for most other wildflowers.

directions: Desert princesplume is a shrubby, short-lived perennial mustard of dry washes, badlands, and disturbed ground scattered through Great Basin sagebrush steppe, instantly recognizable for its dense, foot-long plumes of small bright-yellow flowers topping gray-green, deeply lobed leaves. It is a notable selenium accumulator and often marks seleniferous or alkaline soils where few other showy wildflowers persist, making it a useful indicator species as well as an ornamental. Plants need sharply drained, mineral soil in full sun and little to no summer water, and they tend to be short-lived, re-seeding readily to maintain a population over time. Allow some seedpods to mature and shatter each year rather than deadheading every stalk, to keep a self-sustaining stand going.
